context: A roughly 25 minute recruiter phone screen in which Corvella Health recruiter Theo Lindqvist pitches a Senior Product Designer role to candidate Maya Okafor, covering company, role, compensation, logistics and interview process. Near the end Theo patches in hiring manager Dana Whitfield for a few minutes, who changes one interview stage before dropping off.

facts.statement: Corvella Health builds care coordination software for home health agencies; its main product is Corvella Connect, which handles clinicians' schedules, routes, visit notes and medication reconciliation and syncs to the agency and physician.
Corvella Connect has a clinician mobile app and an agency web console; a payer portal has just been started and is early.
Corvella is used by about 340 home health agencies, mostly in the Mountain West and Midwest.
Corvella is Series B, having closed a $42 million round in March led by Harborline Ventures.
The Series B money is mostly going into product and engineering hiring.
Corvella has about 215 employees (crossed 215 last month).
facts.notes: supersedes the 180 figure stated at line 24

facts.statement: Theo Lindqvist is a senior recruiter at Corvella Health and ran the screen.
The role is Senior Product Designer, which maps to Corvella's P4 level.
The role sits on the Clinician Experience team, which owns the mobile app nurses use in the field.
The role reports to Dana Whitfield, Director of Product Design, who is the hiring manager.
The Clinician Experience team currently has two other designers, a PM, and about 7 engineers.
The team's big project for next year is rebuilding the visit documentation flow; nurses currently spend about 40 minutes after every shift catching up on notes, a burnout driver.
The clinician app must work offline in low-signal areas and sync later.
Dana's first-year success measure for the hire is cutting post-shift documentation time in half, from roughly 40 minutes to 20.
Maya Okafor has about five years as a product designer, starting with about two years at Denver agency Northpaw Studio.
Maya has spent the last three years at Brightlane Insurance as a senior product designer on the claims team.
Maya's mobile claims redesign cut auto claim filing time from about 11 minutes to a median of about 4 minutes and raised mobile completion 22% in the first quarter after launch.
Maya was lead designer on the claims redesign (with one other designer, a researcher and the PM) and ran about 30 usability sessions.
Maya's motivation: her mother has been a home health nurse for about twenty years, so a role focused on nurses' documentation resonates.
Brightlane is moving everyone to three days a week in office starting January, and Maya prefers remote work.
Maya wants to work closely with research and engineering rather than handing designs over the wall.
Onboarding includes two or three ride-alongs with nurses in the first month; engineers also go on ride-alongs.
Corvella has eleven designers across product and no dedicated design system team; it is a shared guild informally run by staff designer Donna Park.
Corvella has one full-time UX researcher, Keiko, shared across the product org; designers run many of their own studies.
The role is hybrid, not fully remote: 2 days a week in the Denver office, Tuesdays and Thursdays for the Clinician Experience team.
facts.notes: corrects Maya's assumption at line 53 that the role is fully remote

facts.statement: Theo said he will get the 'remote-friendly' wording in the job posting fixed.
The Denver office is in LoDo near Union Station.
Employees must be based in Colorado and keep core hours of 10am to 3pm Mountain time.
The base salary band for Senior Product Designer (P4) is $148,000 to $172,000.
facts.notes: supersedes the $128,000-$146,000 band at line 82, which was the P3 band

facts.statement: Maya's target base salary is about $165,000, which Theo noted as within the band.
The annual bonus target is 10% of base, tied to company goals.
Last year the bonus paid out at 100% of target.
The standard equity grant at this level is 12,000 stock options with four-year vesting and a one-year cliff.
The option strike price is based on the last 409A, about $3.10 a share, but a new 409A is coming after the round.
Equity refresh grants are tied to annual performance reviews in February; exact refresh amounts vary.
Benefits: company covers 90% of premiums for the employee and 70% for dependents; 401k with a 4% match.
PTO is unlimited with a mandatory minimum of 15 days.
Maya is on an H-1B through Brightlane and needs a transfer; Corvella supports H-1B transfers.
Corvella uses an outside immigration firm for H-1B transfers.
Maya's notice period at Brightlane is three weeks.
facts.notes: corrects 'two weeks' said at the start of line 104

facts.statement: Maya has a pre-booked, non-negotiable trip to Lisbon for her sister's wedding from October 9 through October 19.
The process has four stages total; the recruiter screen is stage one.
Stage two is a 45 minute interview with hiring manager Dana Whitfield.
Donna Park is a Staff Product Designer on the team, distinct from Dana Whitfield (the hiring manager).

Stage four is the final loop of three sessions: a 60 minute design critique with Donna, a 45 minute cross-functional interview with the PM and engineering lead, and a 30 minute values conversation with someone outside product.
The final loop is usually held in person at the Denver office.
Dana dropped the take-home exercise; stage three is now a 60 minute portfolio review where Maya presents two case studies to Dana, Donna Park and PM Luis Ferrante.
facts.notes: supersedes the 4-hour take-home stage at line 118

facts.statement: Maya may redact NDA-covered numbers and screens from her Brightlane work in the portfolio review.
Maya will send her portfolio link and the two case studies she wants to present to Theo by Friday the 25th.
Maya will send Theo her availability for the next two weeks by Thursday, to pass to Dana for her interview.
Dana Whitfield will send the calendar invite for her hiring manager interview herself.
facts.notes: owner changed from Theo (line 113) to Dana (line 159)

facts.statement: Theo will send Maya the benefits guide PDF by end of day today.
Theo will send calendar invites for the portfolio review and the final loop once dates are locked.
The whole team is at an offsite the week of November 9.
Plan: Dana's interview next week and the portfolio review the week of October 5, before Maya leaves on the 9th.
The final loop will be on October 21 or 22, after Maya returns (she prefers not the 20th since she lands on the 19th).
The team aims to make a hiring decision by October 23.
facts.notes: implicit supersession of the October 16 target at line 124

facts.statement: The target start date is November 16, accounting for three weeks notice, the H-1B transfer paperwork and the November 9 offsite; Maya agreed.
facts.notes: implicit supersession of the November 2 start at line 124

facts.statement: Maya would forfeit her Brightlane annual bonus if she leaves before March.
Corvella's HR manager left last month, so ownership of the premium processing question in people ops is unclear.
Theo describes Dana as direct, holding weekly one on ones and protecting the team's research time.

corrections.initial_value: 4-hour take-home design exercise, 5 days to complete
corrections.final_value: 60 minute portfolio review presenting two case studies

corrections.what: Owner of the hiring manager interview calendar invite

corrections.initial_value: fully remote (Maya's assumption from the posting)
corrections.final_value: hybrid, 2 days a week in the Denver office (Tue/Thu)

not_decisions.statement: Considering Maya for a possible Design Lead role on the payer portal team in Q1 (not approved, no promises)
A sign-on bonus to offset Maya's forfeited Brightlane bonus (floated, not committed; deferred to offer stage)
Having new hires come into the office a third day per week during their first month for onboarding (Dana thinking out loud, not decided)
Moving the team's office days from Tuesday/Thursday to Monday/Wednesday next year (up in the air)
Doing the final loop virtually instead of in person (requested by Maya, no answer)
A chat between Maya and one of the team's designers (offered as an idea; Maya will think about it)

The false assumption that the role is fully remote
